answer:
The handbook's Communication tier list ranks public, written, asynchronous channels best and interruptive ones worst. It's partly a joke. Pull requests are S tier, the best. Requests for comments and GitHub issues are A tier [1]. Public Slack channels are B tier, private messages are D tier, and email is E tier [1]. The worst, F tier, is tapping someone on the shoulder and saying "You got a minute?" [1]

The rest of the handbook backs this up. Slack is for more informal communication, and you should chat publicly by default [2]. Too much context in a private place can hurt contributors who don't have Slack access [3]. Email is also described as one of the worst ways to reach the ICP [4].

The excerpts describe these stages in order: a culture screen, a technical screen, a culture and motivation chat, and the SuperDay. They don't give one numbered list, so I put the order together from the sections. The page also mentions "stage 3 & stage 4" without saying which stages those are.

1. Culture screen: the Talent team runs it, normally as a 20-30 minute call. It is an initial assessment of fit for the job, culture and communication style, and it also sorts out logistics [1].
2. Technical screen: an hour-long technical interview with one of our engineers [2].
3. Culture & motivation chat: a short 15-minute chat with Tim or James, depending on scheduling [3].
4. SuperDay: the final stage, a paid full day of work [4]. The engineering SuperDay guide says it includes a project, a 45-minute debugging session, a check-in call with the SuperDay buddy, and a short chat with a co-founder or exec [5].

The handbook doesn't say whether the culture and motivation chat comes before or after the technical screen. I listed it after based on the order of the sections.

answer:
PostHog uses a context-based expense policy, not hard rules. Use your judgment, and keep the documentation requirements below.

- **Test:** Ask whether you can clearly explain why the expense is in PostHog's best interest, and whether you'd be comfortable explaining it to the whole team publicly. If you're in doubt, ask your team lead for context, not permission [1][2].
- **Limits and cards:** Each person gets a $5,000 monthly User Limit in Brex. It covers individual subscriptions, coworking, equipment, training and similar items. Laptops and Mac Studio Monitors are the exception [3]. Use Brex or Revolut for all work expenses, not a personal card [4].
- **UK:** Use Revolut if the expense is over £75 and has UK VAT. Otherwise use Brex [5].
- **Receipts:** Expenses over $75 or £75 need itemized receipts and a memo within 14 days [6].
- **Transparency:** All expenses are visible company-wide, and team leads get monthly reports [7]. Finance reviews all expenses over $1000, a random sample of smaller Brex expenses, and all Revolut expenses [8].
- **Inappropriate spend:** Personal expenses, such as entertainment subscriptions, are not allowed. Deliberately inappropriate spending will probably be treated as serious misconduct [9].
- **Software:** There needs to be a very significant upside to introducing new collaborative software [10].
- **Travel:** The default is economy [11].

**Manager?** No. Team leads don't automatically manage the team [1]. Each person's line manager is normally their role's functional leader, so engineers report to an engineer whichever small team they're on [2]. Management is minimal, and managers shouldn't set tasks for people in small teams [2].

- **Time and focus:** Side gigs should by default be done in your personal time and must not impact your PostHog work [1]. PostHog must be your main focus, not just a paycheck [2]. It also doesn't offer part-time work [2].
- **Sign-off:** Check in with the relevant Exec team member for your team (James, Tim or Charles) before going ahead [3]. If the gig existed before you joined, this is usually covered in onboarding [3].
- **IP:** PostHog won't claim IP you create in your personal time [4]. Don't bring PostHog's non-open-source IP into your outside work. Only explicitly MIT-licensed PostHog material is fine to use [4].
- **Ideas that start at PostHog:** Anything that comes out of your PostHog work (hackathons, offsites, team projects) is treated as PostHog work by default [5]. To spin it out, get explicit sign-off first [5].
- **Turning it into your full-time job:** If you want your side gig to become your full-time work one day, tell PostHog so you can make a plan [6].

answer:
Sign commits with either Secretive or 1Password. The handbook slightly prefers Secretive because it stores the key in the macOS Secure Enclave, so the key can't be exported, even by malware [1].

Secretive setup:
1. In Secretive, create a new key named "Git signing key" with Protection Level set to Notify [2].
2. Go to Secretive > Integrations > Git Signing and pick that key from the Secret dropdown [2].
3. Paste the ~/.gitconfig and ~/.gitallowedsigners snippets into those files. If ~/.gitconfig already has content, merge them in instead of replacing it [2].
4. Set SSH_AUTH_SOCK for your shell as Secretive instructs [2].
5. Copy your public key. The path is the signingkey in ~/.gitconfig [2].
6. Add it in your GitHub SSH keys settings with the key type set to Signing Key [2].
7. Test it. Make an empty commit on a new branch with `git commit --allow-empty -m "test signing"`, then push it. You should see a green Verified badge [3].

1Password: follow the 1Password git commit signing guide [4].

After setup, turn on "Flag unsigned commits as unverified" in your GitHub profile [5].

Troubleshooting: if Touch ID prompts you on every commit, your key's Protection Level is Require Authentication. Generate a new key with Notify [6].

Paste your public key and set the key type to Signing Key.
Push the branch to GitHub — you should see a green Verified badge on the commit.
Follow the 1Password git commit signing guide.
Once commit signing is configured, enable the option in your GitHub Profile to "Flag unsigned commits as unverified".

answer:
Yes, in most cases. Events and properties can't be edited once they're in Clickhouse, so the way to do a targeted removal is to delete the person profile tied to the affected events. Before any deletion, the customer must stop sending the sensitive data, or it will keep arriving.

- **Stop the leak first.** They should redact client-side or set up a CDP transformation [1].
- **Delete the person profile.** This can be done in the app or via the API [2]. The profile goes immediately, but the events can take days or even weeks to be removed [2].
- **No person profiles?** Then this method isn't available, and they'd have to delete the entire project containing the sensitive data [3].
- **Customers spending $20K+ a year.** The Clickhouse team may be able to craft a targeted deletion or property amendment query, with no guarantees [4]. Escalate a support ticket with the event and property names. Ideally include a SQL query that identifies the data, and check that its numbers match what the customer expects [4]. This can also take days or weeks [4].
- **Immediate removal.** The only way is to delete the project [5].

citations.quote: Before taking any deletion action, they should ensure that they are no longer sending the sensitive data to us either by redacting information client-side or setting up a CDP transformation.

To close it: once you've identified the root cause, implemented a fix, and confirmed customer-facing services are back to normal, type /inc close in the incident channel [1]. Also mark the incident as resolved on the status page [1].

For a major incident's post-mortem:
1. Fill out the template in the incident page. You'll be prompted to do this when the incident is resolved [2].
2. Fill out the Summary and DERP sections in detail, because these are the most valuable [2].
3. Check the timeline is accurate [2].
4. Schedule a team call and invite engineering@posthog.com and key stakeholders [2].
5. Review as a group and update the post-mortem as you go [2].
6. Share the outcome in #incidents. This should happen automatically when you mark the post-mortem as complete [2].

After closing, the incident lead should step away and hand off outstanding customer communications before the post-mortem [3]. Some incidents also need a public post-mortem, for example ones with permanent data impact, ones that directly disrupt customers' own services, or ones with extended unavailability [4]. The public version goes through an internal review before it's published [4].

**Who maintains the SDKs:** A small dedicated SDK team (@PostHog/team-client-libraries) helps drive direction and coordination, but maintenance is shared across engineering [1]. Maintainers are engineers from different teams who volunteer for the SDK support rotation, contribute improvements when their product needs SDK changes, or pick up SDK work on hack days or with spare capacity [2].

**What you do as SDK Support Hero (one person per week):**
- Make sure SDK questions get attention across all SDKs, including mobile [3]. Watch escalated SDK tickets in Zendesk and new issues in the SDK repos (posthog-js, posthog-python, posthog-ios, posthog-android, posthog-flutter, and others) [3].
- Route first. If a specific team is relevant, assign the Zendesk ticket to that team and use the team's GitHub label. If no team fits, label the GitHub issue SDK Support Hero [4].
- Then work on SDK Zendesk tickets and GitHub issues labelled SDK Support Hero (or unlabelled, which you should label). Use your judgement on effort, reward, urgency and your skill set [5].
- Prioritise mobile issues for faster turnaround, because mobile fixes can take weeks or months to roll out. Validate carefully and avoid breaking changes, since mistakes are hard to correct after release [6].
- At the end of the week, post a public handover message in #support-client-libraries covering work in progress, how the rotation is going, and any learnings or feedback [7].

Your first three months of commission are paid at 100% fixed OTE, counted from your start date. Starting July 21st is after the 15th, so you get a split ramp (this is the handbook's own example, for someone who joined 7/21/2025):
- Q3: July isn't counted, since you weren't employed for that month. August and September are paid at 100% fixed OTE [3][4].
- Q4: October is paid at 100% fixed OTE. November and December are paid on your actual attainment against quota [2][4].

The handbook's rule for a start after the 15th gives the same pattern. Its example is a Jan 17th start, which gets two months of 100% fixed OTE in Q1 and one month in Q2. The other two months of Q2 are on quota'ed commission [1].

- They must share a copy of their current contract, pricing or bank statement as proof [2].
- They must sign an annual PostHog contract worth $20k+/year, paid up front. It starts when their current contract expires [2].
- Free usage in the overlap must be proportionate to the contract they sign. For example, a $50k contract with 6 months left gets $25k of free credit [3].
- The competitor must be 'real'. As a rule of thumb, anyone we've written a comparison article about counts [3].
- We have final discretion on who gets the deal [3].
- We can still offer a standard 2-4 week free trial before they sign [3].

Refund handling has four parts: which scenarios qualify, who must meet which criteria, how to calculate and issue the refund, and when to escalate.

**Scenarios and eligibility**
- We refund or credit for four scenarios: learning curve, unexpected stardom, under attack, and wrong setup. Learning curve, for example, applies when it's the first bill over $1 [1].
- The request must be made within 30 days of the billing date [2]. The customer must give a reasonable explanation that fits one of the scenarios [3]. The account must show no signs of fraud or abuse [4].
- For volume spikes, the unusual usage must have stopped and the customer must have taken measures such as a billing limit [5].
- Repeat incidents: for subsequent incidents, check whether the customer acted on our earlier recommendations. If they haven't, offer a partial refund of up to 50% while they fix it. From the third incident on, refunds may be declined [6].

**Channels**
- In-app tickets are reviewed by Support, who issue the refund or credit and reply to the customer [7].
- Contact-sales form or sales email requests can be sent to Support by AEs using the ticket emoji [8].
- For large accounts, the AE may lead the conversation and loop in Support or RevOps [9].

**Calculating the amount**
- Review the customer's usage and set a baseline from the past three months' average [10].
- Subtract the baseline from the spike to get the overage [11].
- Use the pricing calculator or QuoteHog to price the baseline and the baseline plus overage, then take the difference. Don't price the overage on its own, because of tiered pricing [12].

**Refund or credit**
- If the period hasn't ended and the invoice isn't finalized, issue credits [13].
- If the invoice is finalized and it's a first-time request, issue a refund via a credit note. Don't use the refund button [14].

**Issuing**
- Refunds are initiated through Billing Admin and finalized in Stripe via a credit note [15].
- Refund amounts must be allocated manually per product [16].
- Add a note to the Zendesk ticket with your calculation breakdown [17].

**Escalate to RevOps** if something seems off, there have been multiple recent refunds, the case isn't a simple one, the customer is big ($1,667+ monthly), or an invoice needs creating or modifying [18].

answer:
Yes, a trial fits, provided the prospect meets the trial criteria. Make it 2 weeks, and ask for something in return if they want more time.

**Offer a trial?** A $40K deal is above the $20K sales-assist threshold, so it qualifies on that point [1]. Also check that there are clear decision makers and a timeline, that the customer wants technical validation, and that they're ready to invest time in an evaluation [1]. Skip the trial if there's no clear timeline or decision process, they're only price shopping, or they've already committed to buying [2].

**Length:** The default is 2 weeks for $20–60K ARR [3]. Go to 4 weeks only if there's a compelling reason, such as a deal over $60K ARR, a complex technical environment, multiple stakeholders to validate, or the prospect evaluating other products alongside PostHog [4].

**Before you start:** The SDK must be installed and events firing before the trial proceeds [5]. You also need documented success criteria and a documented timeline [6].

**If they ask for more time:** Extensions are common, and we're happy to grant them [7]. An extension is typically 7–30 days, and we should ask for something in return [7]. Examples are:
- an introduction to key stakeholders
- a commitment to start procurement in parallel
- verbal confirmation they're moving forward
- weekly check-in calls until the trial ends

Also find out why they need more time and what specifically needs to be accomplished [7].

answer:
Short version: you need to be switched off in both Salesforce and Default, and the calibration fields stop you being flooded when you return.

**Stopping leads while you're away**
- Being out doesn't stop routing by default. Leads still go to you unless you're removed from the round robin [1].
- For more than 1 day off, tell Mine or Simon 2 working days before you leave. They set you to inactive on the Leads assignment tracker in Salesforce and set a reminder to re-add you [2].
- In Salesforce, the Is Active checkbox on the lead assignment tracker is unchecked so you get no new leads [3].
- In Default (app → routing → queues), your status is toggled to Inactive in each queue you're in [4]. Setting yourself as Out of Office in your Default personal settings does not stop assignments, so the queue toggle is still needed [5].
- Because you're off more than 5 days, you should be turned off 2 days before you leave. You're turned back on the day you return [6].
- Update your calendar with your time off so Default doesn't schedule meetings while you're out [7].

**Will you be flooded on return?**
No, as long as the calibration is done. While you're inactive, others keep getting leads and their totals rise. Before you're reactivated, the gap is added to your Calibration column in Default. Salesforce has the same adjustment in the Manual Lead Adjustment column. For example, if others got +10 each, you get +10, so you aren't handed 10 leads the moment you're reactivated [8].

answer:
You have two options.

1. Automatic transition offer: when the credits are fully used or expire, the team moves to a standard paid plan. They get an email about it and a one-time $500 credit bonus to soften the transition [1].

2. Prepaid deal with free credits (sales-led): offer two months of free credit if they sign a prepaid deal [2]. The offer runs until the first billing date after the credits expire. If they use up their credits early, they still have until the original expiration date to claim it [2]. The steps are:
- Review their average monthly cost and estimate 12 months of coverage (monthly cost x 12) [3].
- They buy credits for about 12 months of usage, expiring 12 months after the contract start date, and get about 2 months of extra usage free, applied before the contract start date [3].
- If they buy fewer credits, they get an extra 1/6 of the amount they buy, for free [3].
- The free credits are one-time only [4]. Note them in the order form's special terms using the standard wording [4].

Also, extending the credit window itself isn't usual. Extensions are only for exceptional cases, and Customer Success reviews them manually [5].

Set up a trial in the billing admin. You'll need access to billing.posthog.com, and the customer needs an Organization on EU or US Cloud. Because they already pay, you also need the extra steps below.

1. Log in to Billing with Google SSO, click Trials in the left sidebar, then click Add Trial. Fill in the form: customer, status Active, target (paid, teams or enterprise, whichever you need), type Standard, and an expiration date. Then click Save [1].
2. Pick a length. 2 weeks is the usual default for deals worth $20-60k, and 4 weeks is for $60k+ deals [2][3]. A customer who is going to exceed the free tier quickly can be given 2 weeks of free usage through the billing service [4].
3. For existing paid subscriptions, ask Mine to update Stripe and billing admin so revenue numbers are unaffected and the customer isn't billed during the trial [5].
4. Then do the following [5]:
   - Remove the Stripe Subscription ID in Billing Admin, but keep the Stripe Customer ID.
   - Set all products in the product map to a free status.
   - Cancel the subscription in Stripe.
   - Create a new subscription before the trial ends and update Billing Admin, so the customer's experience isn't affected when they go back to paying.
5. When the trial date passes, their features reset to the free plan unless they have subscribed in that time [1].

Extensions are possible only in exceptional cases. When credits run out, you move to standard paid billing, and there are some offers to soften the move.

**More time:**
- The 12-month window is meant to be firm, so credits usually aren't extended. Exceptional cases are considered [1].
- You'd need to explain clearly why you couldn't use the credit in time and show evidence of recent progress or changes. Customer Success reviews requests manually [2].
- Small open source projects without corporate backing and under $200k annual revenue can contact support to have the 12-month expiry waived [3].

**What happens at expiry or when credits are used up:**
- Credits are valid for 12 months from application. After they expire or are fully used, you're moved to standard billing [4]. This is automatic, and you get an email about it plus a one-time $500 credit bonus to soften the transition [5].
- Before expiry you get milestone emails at 50%, 75% and 100% usage, and when credits expire [5].

**Prepaid offer for startups:**
- Startups signing a prepaid deal can get two months of free credit. The offer lasts until the first billing date after the credits expire. If you use up your credits early, you still have until the original expiration date to claim it [6].
- Free credits are typically ~2 months of usage when you buy ~12 months of prepaid credits. If you buy fewer, you get an extra 1/6 of the amount you buy [7].

To find a customer, start by asking the PM for that product, since PMs do lots of user interviews and can suggest warm leads. You can also post in company Slack channels, with context on what you're looking for [2].

Steps after that:
- Before reaching out, search for the company in Vitally. If an Account Executive or CSM is assigned, give them a heads-up. If nobody is assigned, you can reach out directly [2].

What makes a good story: it should show that PostHog helped them achieve meaningful results and that they represent who we build for. Payment status, using every product, and brand recognition don't matter [2]. Case studies live in /contents/customers/ and appear on posthog.com/customers [2].
